meta.title: Who really said "Can't Act; Slightly Bald; Can Dance a Little"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Astaire did not say it. An anonymous studio reader wrote it about his screen test. Earliest print: 1937; the familiar wording: Fortune, August 1939.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Can't Act; Slightly Bald; Can Dance a Little'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Fred Astaire but a nameless studio evaluator, writing about him. Earliest known printing 1937; the familiar wording appeared in Fortune, August 1939.

answer.label: Not by Fred Astaire — an anonymous studio verdict written about him
answer.sourceLine: This was never Astaire’s line: it is a studio reader’s verdict on him, scrawled on the report card after an early-1930s screen test, and the writer has never been reliably identified. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the familiar three-part wording to Fortune magazine of August 1939, which credits it only to “some hapless underling”; the earliest printing it found, an Associated Press column of 16 June 1937, is shorter still, and Astaire’s own version differed again.

source.heading: The paper trail

docMeta.dd: Robbin Coons (Associated Press), The Canton Repository, 16 June 1937
An unidentified studio reader — “some hapless underling”; the report itself is lost
“Can’t act. Slightly bald. Also dances.” — ABC 20/20 interview, 1980

source.excerpt: During his illness, Deanna Durbin and Fred Astaire were tested at Culver City, and turned down. On the subject of Astaire, some hapless underling scrawled on his report card, “Can’t act; slightly bald; can dance a little.”
trail: The earliest printing Quote Investigator located ↗ is an Associated Press column by Robbin Coons in The Canton Repository of 16 June 1937, and the verdict there is shorter and looser: “Slightly bald and can dance a little,” said of a report card on Astaire, “who made his first film at M-G-M.”

The wording we all know turns up in Fortune’s August 1939 article on Loew’s Inc., where “some hapless underling scrawled” it on Astaire’s report card after a Culver City test. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that this version — repeated in 1946 and 1958 accounts of the document Astaire kept — has the most support, while the precise wording remains unclear.

Astaire’s own version was different again: “Can’t act. Slightly bald. Also dances,” which he gave in a 1980 ABC 20/20 interview with Barbara Walters, as recorded by Wikipedia ↗ and Wikiquote ↗, the latter noting he reaffirmed it in Bob Thomas’s Astaire, the Man, the Dancer (1985).

The one screen-test document that demonstrably survives says the opposite: David O. Selznick’s memo of 26 January 1933 backed Astaire — “his charm is so tremendous that it comes through even in this wretched test” — printed in Rudy Behlmer’s Memo from David O. Selznick ↗ (Viking, 1972) and cited by Quote Investigator at page 51 ↗.
source.excerptNote: The illness is Irving Thalberg’s: Fortune’s point was that MGM’s key decision-maker was away when Astaire was assessed and rejected. This passage, quoted by Quote Investigator ↗, is the earliest appearance it found of the three-part wording people quote today.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can be asserted for the memo itself: it is an unpublished internal studio document by an unidentified writer, it no longer exists, and its exact wording is unsettled. The wording survives only through later periodicals — the 1937 Associated Press column and Fortune of August 1939 — both published well after 1930 and both with corporate rights holders, so quotle.info makes no public-domain claim here.

author.name: Fred Astaire
author.kicker: About the subject of the line
author.heading: The man it was written about
author.metaLine: 1899–1987 · American dancer, singer, actor and choreographer
author.bio: Born Frederick Austerlitz in Omaha, Nebraska, Astaire spent his childhood and youth in vaudeville and then on Broadway and the London stage with his sister Adele, before a solo film career that made him, by common consent, the greatest popular dancer ever filmed. He is the subject of this line, not its author — and he told the story against himself for decades, keeping the report as a memento and correcting the wording when asked. He insisted on his own innovations too: dances shot in long takes with the dancers in full view, and numbers written into the plot rather than staged as spectacle.

misattribution.heading: What the popular version gets wrong
misattribution.intro: Almost every element of the way this line is usually repeated — who said it, what it said, and which studio said it — is either unsupported or contested.

items.why: It is a verdict written about Astaire, not by him. He is the subject of the sentence; the writer was an anonymous studio reader whom Quote Investigator ↗ could not identify.

The four-part version — “Can’t act. Can’t sing. Slightly bald. Can dance a little.” — appears in Leslie Halliwell’s The Filmgoer’s Book of Quotes (1973). None of the 1937–1963 citations collected by Quote Investigator ↗ contains “Can’t sing.”

The modern folklore version calls it an RKO report, as Wikipedia ↗ records. But the 1930s press placed it at MGM: the 1937 AP column notes Astaire “made his first film at M-G-M,” Fortune puts the test at Culver City, and a 1958 item calls the surviving keepsake a “yellowed MGM interoffice studio memo” dated 1933 — all quoted by Quote Investigator ↗, which does not resolve the conflict.

Grady is named only in Debbie Reynolds’s 1988 memoir Debbie: My Life, recalling a 1949 meeting, and repeated in Peter J. Levinson’s 2009 Astaire biography — both summarised by Quote Investigator ↗, and neither is contemporary evidence. Their wordings differ from each other and from Fortune’s.

Pandro S. Berman, who produced the Astaire–Rogers pictures, said he had never heard the story in the 1930s and that it surfaced years later, per Wikipedia ↗, citing John Mueller’s Astaire Dancing (p. 7).

misattribution.truthLine: There is good evidence that some dismissive studio verdict on Astaire existed in the early 1930s — he kept the document and showed it to reporters — but the exact words are unsettled and the writer is unknown. Quote Investigator ↗ judges the Fortune phrasing the best-supported; Astaire himself said it read “Can’t act. Slightly bald. Also dances.”

context.heading: Why the story stuck
lead: It is the perfect Hollywood parable: the bureaucrat who could not see genius standing in front of him, and the genius who kept the evidence on his wall. That is exactly how it circulated. A 1946 Woman’s Home Companion column described Astaire clearing out his dressing room and producing his “favorite memento” — the casting director’s report on his first screen test — and a 1958 item placed a yellowed studio memo over his fireplace in Beverly Hills.

The catch is that the anecdote grew in the retelling while the paper shrank out of existence. The verdict got a fourth clause it never had in the 1930s; the studio migrated from MGM to RKO; a name was finally attached to the writer half a century later, by someone recalling a conversation. And when Astaire was asked directly, in a 1980 television interview, his own memory of the line was the shortest version of all.
context.detailsSummary: The MGM / RKO tangle, and the one memo that survives
detailsBody: The confusion has a plausible root. Astaire was signed to RKO, where David O. Selznick commissioned his test in January 1933, but his Hollywood debut was a loan-out to MGM for Dancing Lady that same year — so 1930s writers describing an MGM report card and later writers describing an RKO one may both be half-right. Neither Quote Investigator nor Wikipedia settles it, and neither should this page.

What is not in doubt is the memo Selznick actually wrote on 26 January 1933, to an assistant named Philip Siff: “I am a little uncertain about the man, but I feel, in spite of his enormous ears and bad chin line, that his charm is so tremendous that it comes through even in this wretched test.” It is the mirror image of the famous line — a genuine, dated, published document in which the executive backs Astaire — and it is far less quoted.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest evidence QI located is a 16 June 1937 Associated Press column by Robbin Coons in The Canton Repository reading "Slightly bald and can dance a little", and the familiar three-part wording "Can't act; slightly bald; can dance a little" first appears in Fortune, August 1939, credited to "some hapless underling" after a Culver City test; QI concludes the precise wording is unclear but the Fortune version has the most support.

QI's chronology also records the 1946 Woman's Home Companion memento anecdote, the 1958 Reader's Digest item describing a yellowed MGM interoffice memo dated 1933 over Astaire's fireplace, Leslie Halliwell's 1973 four-part version including "Can't sing", Debbie Reynolds's 1988 naming of Burt Grady, Levinson's 2009 biography, and Selznick's 26 January 1933 memo at page 51 of Memo from David O. Selznick.

Wikipedia states the RKO screen-test report is lost, that Pandro S. Berman said he never heard the story in the 1930s and it emerged years afterward, that Astaire insisted the report read "Can't act. Slightly bald. Also dances" in a 1980 ABC 20/20 interview with Barbara Walters, and gives Selznick's "enormous ears and bad chin line ... wretched test" memo; it gives Astaire's birth name as Frederick Austerlitz, born 10 May 1899 in Omaha, Nebraska, died 22 June 1987.

Wikiquote lists "Can't act, slightly bald, also dances." under its "Hollywood on Astaire" section, sourced to Astaire's version of the lost screen test report given in his 1980 20/20 interview with Barbara Walters and reaffirmed in Bob Thomas, Astaire, the Man, the Dancer (Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 1985), p. 78.

This Internet Archive item is a lending copy of Memo from David O. Selznick, edited by Rudy Behlmer, published by The Viking Press, New York, 1972 — the edition that prints Selznick's January 1933 memo about Astaire.

This Google Books volume is the issue of LIFE magazine dated 25 August 1941 (the issue QI cites for the "Can't act. Slightly bald. Can dance a little." passage); the fetch confirmed the issue identity but did not surface the snippet text itself.
